recipe: Structure your effect so the body describes how to start synchronization and the returned cleanup function describes how to stop it.
trigger_condition: When writing any useEffect that interacts with an external system such as a server connection or subscription.
evidence: Your Effect's body specifies how to **start synchronizing:**
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Write each effect to handle a single start/stop cycle, independent of whether the component is mounting, updating, or unmounting.
trigger_condition: When designing effects that depend on props or state that change over time.
evidence: Instead, always focus on a single start/stop cycle at a time. It shouldn't matter whether a component is mounting, updating, or unmounting. All you need to do is to describe how to start synchronization and how to stop it.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Use React's linter rule to verify that your effect's dependency array is correct so the effect stays synchronized to the latest props and state.
trigger_condition: When writing effects with a dependency array.
evidence: React provides a linter rule to check that you've specified your Effect's dependencies correctly. This keeps your Effect synchronized to the latest props and state.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Avoid thinking of effects as callbacks or lifecycle events tied to specific component lifecycle moments, as this mental model becomes complicated quickly.
trigger_condition: When designing or debugging effects that behave unexpectedly across multiple re-renders.
evidence: When you looked from the component's perspective, it was tempting to think of Effects as "callbacks" or "lifecycle events" that fire at a specific time like "after a render" or "before unmount". This way of thinking gets complicated very fast, so it's best to avoid.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Split unrelated logic into separate Effects rather than combining them in one Effect just because they need to run at the same time.
trigger_condition: You are tempted to add unrelated logic (e.g., analytics logging) to an existing Effect simply because it needs to run alongside it.
evidence: Each Effect in your code should represent a separate and independent synchronization process.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Include all reactive values (props, state, and values calculated from them) that your Effect reads in its dependency array.
trigger_condition: Your Effect reads props, state variables, or values derived from them that may change across re-renders.
evidence: Reactive values must be included in dependencies
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Do not include values that never change across re-renders (e.g., module-level constants) in your Effect's dependency array.
trigger_condition: A value used by your Effect is a constant that remains the same regardless of how many times the component re-renders.
evidence: Since `serverUrl` never changes, it wouldn't make sense to specify it as a dependency. After all, dependencies only do something when they change over time!
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: When determining your Effect's dependency array, include every variable declared in the component body that the Effect uses, since all such variables are reactive.
trigger_condition: You are deciding which variables to list as dependencies for an Effect that reads multiple variables from the component scope.
evidence: This is why all variables from the component body used by the Effect should be in the Effect dependency list.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: When deciding whether to split or combine Effects, base your decision on whether the logic represents the same process or separate processes, not on whether the code looks cleaner.
trigger_condition: You are evaluating whether to split a cohesive piece of logic into multiple Effects or keep it in one.
evidence: This is why you should think whether the processes are same or separate, not whether the code looks cleaner.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Include every reactive value read inside your useEffect as a dependency, since all values in the component body (props, state, and computed variables) are reactive and can change on re-render.
trigger_condition: When writing a useEffect that reads any value from the component body.
evidence: All values inside the component (including props, state, and variables in your component's body) are reactive. Any reactive value can change on a re-render, so you need to include reactive values as Effect's dependencies.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Do not use mutable values such as location.pathname as useEffect dependencies; instead, read and subscribe to them with useSyncExternalStore.
trigger_condition: When you need to react to an external mutable value that changes outside React's rendering data flow.
evidence: A mutable value like [`location.pathname`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Location/pathname) can't be a dependency.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Do not use ref.current or values read from it as useEffect dependencies, because changing it does not trigger a re-render.
trigger_condition: When you are tempted to list ref.current in your useEffect dependency array.
evidence: A mutable value like [`ref.current`](/reference/react/useRef#reference) or things you read from it also can't be a dependency.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: You may include the ref object returned by useRef itself as a dependency, since the object is stable even though its current property is mutable.
trigger_condition: When you need to reference a ref inside an Effect and want to know what is valid to list.
evidence: The ref object returned by `useRef` itself can be a dependency, but its `current` property is intentionally mutable.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Move values that never change outside the component or inside the Effect body so they are not calculated during rendering and do not need to be listed as dependencies.
trigger_condition: When a value used in an Effect is constant and you want to avoid listing it as a dependency.
evidence: you can move them outside the component. Now they don't need to be dependencies:
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Do not suppress the linter to silence a missing-dependency warning; instead, restructure the code so the value is no longer reactive or no longer needs to be a dependency.
trigger_condition: When adding a linter-suggested dependency causes an infinite loop or excessive re-synchronization.
evidence: Don't fix these problems by suppressing the linter!
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Stable values such as the set function returned by useState or the ref object returned by useRef can be omitted from useEffect dependencies since they are guaranteed not to change on re-render.
trigger_condition: When deciding whether to include set functions or ref objects in your useEffect dependency array.
evidence: Stable values aren't reactive, so you may omit them from the list. Including them is allowed: they won't change, so it doesn't matter.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Add a dependency array to your Effect and include every reactive value used inside it, so the Effect re-synchronizes when those values change.
trigger_condition: You have a useEffect that reads reactive values (state, props) but lacks a dependency array or is missing entries.
evidence: First, add a dependency array. Then, make sure that every reactive value used by the Effect is specified in the array.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: You cannot declare an Effect conditionally (e.g., inside an if block), but you can use conditional logic inside the Effect body to control behavior.
trigger_condition: You want an Effect to only run or only update state under certain conditions.
evidence: You can't declare an Effect conditionally. However, the code inside the Effect can use conditions!
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Avoid suppressing the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps linter rule; if you never suppress it, you will never encounter stale value bugs.
trigger_condition: You see a react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint warning in your useEffect.
evidence: If you never suppress the linter, you will never see problems with stale values.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Move event handler functions inside the useEffect body instead of defining them in the component scope, so the effect depends on the state values you read inside rather than on a reactive function reference.
trigger_condition: Your effect resubscribes on every re-render because it depends on a callback defined outside the effect.
evidence: A better fix would be to move the `handleMove` function *inside* the Effect. Then `handleMove` won't be a reactive value, and so your Effect won't depend on a function.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Include reactive props in your useEffect dependency array rather than suppressing the linter; a prop passed from a parent can change between renders and the effect must re-run to stay in sync.
trigger_condition: A useEffect uses a prop that can change when the parent re-renders, and the linter flags it as a missing dependency.
evidence: The problem is that `createConnection` is a prop, so it's a reactive value. It can change over time! (And indeed, it should--when the user ticks the checkbox, the parent component passes a different value of the `createConnection` prop.)
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Pass a primitive state value (like a boolean) as a prop instead of a function reference, and decide which function to call inside the effect, so the effect only re-runs when the actual state changes rather than on every parent re-render.
trigger_condition: A parent component passes a function as a prop to a child, and the child's effect depends on that prop, causing it to re-run on every parent re-render.
evidence: In this version, the `App` component passes a boolean prop instead of a function. Inside the Effect, you decide which function to use. Since both `createEncryptedConnection` and `createUnencryptedConnection` are declared outside the component, they aren't reactive, and don't need to be dependencies.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Write a separate Effect for each independent synchronization process rather than trying to handle multiple data dependencies in a single Effect.
trigger_condition: When two pieces of state are each synchronized to independent external sources (e.g., one API call for planets and another for places).
evidence: If you have two independent synchronization processes, you need to write two separate Effects.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Do not combine two Effects into one just to reduce code repetition; combining them forces you to merge their dependency arrays, which can cause unnecessary refetches when one dependency changes.
trigger_condition: When you are tempted to merge two separate Effects into a single Effect to avoid writing similar code twice.
evidence: This code is a bit repetitive. However, that's not a good reason to combine it into a single Effect! If you did this, you'd have to combine both Effect's dependencies into one list, and then changing the planet would refetch the list of all planets. Effects are not a tool for code reuse.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Extract repetitive effect logic (fetching data, managing list and selection state) into a custom Hook to reduce duplication across multiple Effects.
trigger_condition: When multiple Effects in your component share the same pattern of fetching data from an API and managing related state.
evidence: Instead, to reduce repetition, you can extract some logic into a custom Hook like `useSelectOptions` below:
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Add an early return guard at the top of your Effect when a dependency variable has not yet been initialized, so the effect does not fire with a stale or empty value.
trigger_condition: When an Effect depends on a state variable that may be an empty string or null on the first render.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Replace most Effects in your application with custom Hooks, whether written by you or adopted from the community, to keep component code clean.
trigger_condition: You find yourself writing Effects directly in components and want to reduce that frequency over time.
evidence: Ideally, most Effects in your application should eventually be replaced by custom Hooks, whether written by you or by the community.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Wrap Effect synchronization logic inside a custom Hook so the calling component does not need to know about the Effect.
trigger_condition: A component's Effect contains synchronization logic that you want to abstract away from the component that uses it.
evidence: Custom Hooks hide the synchronization logic, so the calling component doesn't know about the Effect.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects

recipe: Gradually build up a reusable palette of custom Hooks as you develop your app, so you eventually write Effects in components very rarely.
trigger_condition: You are in the ongoing process of developing an application and want to minimize direct Effect usage in components over time.
evidence: As you keep working on your app, you'll develop a palette of Hooks to choose from, and eventually you won't need to write Effects in your components very often.
source_name: react.dev learn: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects
